error_modes.label: LEVEL OFF ALTITUDE AT PATTERN ALTITUDE

texts.0: SP, due to the absence of a lead point for the level off in the climbing turn, did not arrest the climb at pattern altitude as required by the specific criteria. The aircraft passed more than 300 feet above the assigned pattern altitude and was still climbing when the IP took the controls to stop the overshoot. The return to pattern altitude was flown by the IP and not by SP.
texts.1: SP, due to a late power reduction after the roll out on downwind, did not complete the level off at pattern altitude within tolerance. Altitude reached the 300 feet limit above the assigned value and stayed there until the IP prompted verbally. SP corrected only after that call, so the level off was finished late and the downwind was flown high for several seconds.
texts.2: SP, due to slow relaxation of back pressure during the roll out, did not stop the climb at the assigned pattern altitude on the first attempt. Altitude deviated about 200 feet high, between the 150 and the 300 feet band. SP identified the trend without any prompting and re-established pattern altitude within a few seconds with no IP input.
texts.3: SP set the lead point in good time, reduced power and relaxed back pressure so that the level off was completed within 150 feet of the assigned pattern altitude. Altitude was then held steady while SP re-established downwind spacing. Pitch and power were adjusted in one continuous sequence rather than by successive corrections.
texts.4: SP anticipated the level off and stopped the climb within about 50 feet of pattern altitude, with no overshoot and no secondary correction. Altitude then remained essentially constant for the whole downwind leg. The transition from climb to level flight was made with a single smooth control and power input.
texts.marginal: SP levelled off inside the required tolerance, but each pattern finished about 130 feet above the assigned altitude and needed a small secondary correction to settle. The deviation was in the same direction every time, which shows the lead point is being set late rather than misjudged at random. SP is expected to anticipate the level off earlier so that pattern altitude is captured on the first input.

texts_at.0: SP worked the level-off at pattern altitude, with the IP demonstrating the technique first, a first exposure to this task at this stage of the syllabus. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard, and SP is expected to carry more of the task independently at the next opportunity.
texts_at.1: SP levelled off at pattern altitude inside the code 1 band, the deviation reaching about 280 feet before the aircraft was brought back down. Performance met the desired standard for this stage, and SP is expected to set the lead point for the level off a little earlier so the overshoot is smaller.
texts_at.2: SP levelled off at pattern altitude inside the code 2 band, correcting a deviation of about 220 feet that developed on the roll out from the climbing turn. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training, and SP is expected to reduce power and relax back pressure together rather than in sequence.
texts_at.3: SP set the lead point in good time and completed the level off within about 130 feet of the assigned pattern altitude. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point, and SP is expected to anticipate the level off a little earlier so the capture needs no secondary correction.

texts_above.1: SP levelled off at pattern altitude, the deviation reaching about 280 feet before the aircraft was brought back down. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP recognized the climb continuing past the lead point and re-established pattern altitude within about 220 feet with no IP input, correcting the trend without any prompting. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good level-off technique at pattern altitude.
texts_above.3: SP set the lead point in good time, reduced power and relaxed back pressure so the level off was completed within about 130 feet of the assigned pattern altitude in one continuous sequence rather than by successive corrections. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good level-off technique at pattern altitude.
texts_above.4: SP anticipated the level off and stopped the climb within about 60 feet of pattern altitude, with no overshoot and no secondary correction needed. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to excellent level-off technique at pattern altitude.

error_modes.label: BANK AND AIRSPEED CONTROL DURING THE MANEUVER

texts.0: SP, due to uncoordinated application of bank and back pressure at the initiation of the closed pattern, did not maintain the bank and the airspeeds prescribed by the Flight Manual and the Techniques and Procedures Manual. Bank increased about 25 deg past the briefed value while airspeed decayed well below the value for the turn, and the aircraft arrived on downwind low on energy and displaced from the intended track. The IP reduced bank and reset the flight path before the pattern could be continued.
texts.1: SP, due to chasing the flight path with bank instead of stabilizing pitch first, did not hold the bank and airspeeds of the Techniques and Procedures Manual. Bank varied about 15 deg either side of the briefed value and airspeed sat at the low limit for the turn until the IP called for a correction. SP recovered the parameters only after that verbal input, so the pattern was flown at the edge of the standard throughout.
texts.2: SP, due to a lagging cross-check between attitude and airspeed in the turn, did not hold the briefed bank and airspeed continuously. Bank wandered about 10 deg around the briefed value with a corresponding airspeed excursion, which left the aircraft between the 150 and 300 feet band on the subsequent level off. SP detected both deviations early and re-established the parameters without prompting and without IP action.
texts.3: SP established the briefed bank at the initiation and held it accurately, with airspeed maintained within the values of the Flight Manual and the Techniques and Procedures Manual throughout the turn. The cross-check between attitude, bank and airspeed remained continuous, so corrections were small and made early. The aircraft arrived on downwind on the intended track and on speed.
texts.4: SP flew the closed pattern with the bank set precisely at the briefed value and held it essentially constant, with airspeed steady inside the prescribed range from initiation to roll out. No corrective input beyond trim adjustment was needed at any point of the turn. The aircraft arrived on downwind on speed, on altitude and on the intended track.
texts.marginal: SP kept bank and airspeed inside the standards, but the bank was consistently a few degrees shallow and airspeed drifted toward the low end of the range in the second half of the turn. The pattern remained acceptable only because SP added power late each time. SP is expected to set the briefed bank at the initiation and protect the airspeed with the power setting rather than by unloading the turn.

texts_at.0: SP flew the bank and airspeed control in the pattern, with the IP talking through each step as it was flown, the supporting technique still being built at this point. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage, and SP is expected to rely less on the IP's assistance as the item is repeated.
texts_at.1: SP held the briefed bank and airspeed inside the code 1 band, the resulting level-off deviation reaching about 280 feet before the parameters were corrected. Performance met the desired standard for this stage, and SP is expected to set the briefed bank at the initiation and protect the airspeed with power rather than by unloading the turn.
texts_at.2: SP held the briefed bank and airspeed inside the code 2 band, correcting a level-off deviation of about 220 feet that followed a wandering bank and airspeed in the turn. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training, and SP is expected to keep the cross-check between attitude and airspeed continuous rather than lagging.
texts_at.3: SP established the briefed bank at the initiation and held it accurately, keeping the resulting level-off deviation to about 130 feet. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus, and SP is expected to hold the cross-check a little tighter so the level off needs an even smaller correction.

texts_above.1: SP held the briefed bank and airspeed, the resulting level-off deviation reaching about 280 feet. SP corrected the trend after a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP detected a wandering bank and airspeed early in the turn and re-established the parameters, keeping the resulting level-off deviation to about 220 feet without prompting and without IP action. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound bank and airspeed control in the pattern.
texts_above.3: SP established the briefed bank at the initiation and held it accurately, with airspeed maintained within the prescribed values and the resulting level-off deviation held to about 130 feet through a continuous cross-check. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed bank and airspeed control in the pattern.
texts_above.4: SP flew the closed pattern with the bank set precisely at the briefed value and airspeed steady throughout, keeping the resulting level-off deviation to about 60 feet with no corrective input beyond trim. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to exceptional bank and airspeed control in the pattern.

error_modes.label: DOWNWIND ENTRY, TRAFFIC SEQUENCING AND MINIMUM ENTRY AIRSPEED

texts.0: SP, due to loss of situational awareness of the aircraft position in the pattern, did not enter downwind according to the existing traffic and did not respect the 140 KIAS minimum entry airspeed. The aircraft rolled out on downwind at 126 KIAS and inside the preceding aircraft, with no usable spacing for the following approach. The IP took control to restore separation and to re-establish the aircraft on the correct downwind position.
texts.1: SP, due to degraded situational awareness of the traffic already established in the pattern, did not adjust the closed pattern to the existing traffic and entered downwind at 140 KIAS with no margin. Spacing on the preceding aircraft was reduced to the point where the IP had to call for an extension of the downwind. SP acted only after that call, so the sequence was preserved by verbal direction rather than by SP planning.
texts.2: SP, due to a scan that stayed inside the cockpit during the turn, did not confirm the position of the preceding traffic before initiating the closed pattern. Airspeed on entering downwind was 145 KIAS, above the minimum but with the spacing tighter than briefed. SP identified the closure on the preceding aircraft in good time and adjusted the downwind track and power without prompting and without IP input.
texts.3: SP checked the pattern traffic before initiating and entered downwind clear of the preceding aircraft with an airspeed comfortably above the 140 KIAS minimum. Spacing supported a normal continuation to the following approach with no adjustment required. The lookout was maintained throughout the turn as well as on the downwind.
texts.4: SP built the closed pattern around the traffic already established, timing the initiation so that the downwind entry produced correct spacing with no later adjustment. Airspeed on entering downwind was well above the 140 KIAS minimum and stable. SP kept an accurate picture of every aircraft in the pattern and reported it correctly when asked.
texts.marginal: SP entered downwind above the 140 KIAS minimum and clear of traffic, but the decision to initiate was taken late each time and the spacing came out tighter than briefed. The picture of the preceding aircraft was rebuilt during the turn rather than established before it. SP is expected to confirm the traffic sequence before initiating the closed pattern so that the downwind entry needs no further adjustment.

texts_at.0: SP practiced the downwind entry and traffic sequencing, with the IP providing hands-on guidance on the controls, the sequence still new to SP at this stage of training. The maneuver is being introduced at this point of the syllabus, so no independent standard is required yet, and SP is expected to manage more of the sequence unaided on the next presentation.
texts_at.1: SP entered downwind clear of traffic and above the minimum entry airspeed inside the code 1 band, the resulting altitude on the roll out running about 280 feet off pattern altitude before it was corrected. Performance met the desired standard for this stage, and SP is expected to confirm the traffic sequence before initiating so the downwind entry needs no further adjustment.
texts_at.2: SP entered downwind clear of traffic and above the minimum entry airspeed inside the code 2 band, correcting a downwind track and power discrepancy that had left the altitude about 220 feet off pattern altitude. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training, and SP is expected to check the preceding traffic before initiating the closed pattern rather than during the turn.
texts_at.3: SP checked the pattern traffic before initiating and entered downwind clear of the preceding aircraft above the minimum entry airspeed, holding the resulting altitude within about 130 feet of pattern altitude. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus, and SP is expected to time the initiation a little earlier so the spacing comes out with more margin.

texts_above.1: SP entered downwind clear of traffic and above the minimum entry airspeed, the resulting altitude on the roll out running about 280 feet off pattern altitude. The adjustment followed a verbal call from the IP. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP identified a closure on the preceding aircraft in good time and adjusted the downwind track and power without prompting, keeping the resulting altitude within about 220 feet of pattern altitude and without IP input. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to solid traffic sequencing on the downwind entry.
texts_above.3: SP checked the pattern traffic before initiating and entered downwind clear of the preceding aircraft comfortably above the minimum entry airspeed, holding the resulting altitude within about 130 feet of pattern altitude with spacing that needed no adjustment. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to precise traffic sequencing on the downwind entry.
texts_above.4: SP built the closed pattern around the traffic already established, timing the initiation so the downwind entry produced correct spacing and the resulting altitude stayed within about 60 feet of pattern altitude with no later adjustment. error_modes.label: POWER MANAGEMENT AND ENERGY THROUGH THE PATTERN

texts.0: SP, due to an incomplete power lever movement at the initiation, did not set MAX power as required and did not adjust power afterwards as the pattern demanded. The aircraft entered the turn with a partial power setting and lost the energy required for the climbing turn, arriving below pattern altitude and slow. The IP advanced the power lever and reset the profile before the pattern could be completed.
texts.1: SP, due to setting power by feel instead of confirming the indication, did not set MAX power at the initiation of the closed pattern. Torque remained short of the required value for most of the climbing turn and airspeed decayed to the lower limit until the IP called for power. SP made the correction only after that call, and the level off was consequently reached at the 300 feet tolerance.
texts.2: SP, due to a delayed power reduction after the level off, did not adjust power as required once pattern altitude was reached. The aircraft accelerated through the briefed downwind speed and finished about 200 feet high before the correction took effect. SP recognized the excess energy without prompting and set the correct power to restore both altitude and speed with no IP input.
texts.3: SP set MAX power at the initiation, confirmed the indication and then adjusted power as required at the level off so that the downwind was flown at the briefed setting. Energy through the pattern was managed with anticipation rather than with reactive corrections. Altitude and airspeed were both re-established within tolerance at the same time.
texts.4: SP applied MAX power smoothly and precisely at the initiation and reduced it at exactly the point required for the level off, so that pattern altitude and downwind airspeed were captured together with no overshoot. Power changes were small, timely and matched to the flight path throughout the pattern. No further adjustment was needed during the downwind.
texts.marginal: SP set MAX power at the initiation and adjusted afterwards inside the standards, but the reduction at the level off was made in two steps and slightly late on each pattern. This left a small altitude and speed excursion that had to be corrected on the downwind. SP is expected to plan the power reduction with the level off so that both parameters are captured with a single adjustment.

texts_at.0: SP worked power management through the closed pattern, with the IP walking through the sequence step by step, the pace of the item still unfamiliar at this point. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance, and SP is expected to need less of that guidance on the next presentation.
texts_at.1: SP set and adjusted power through the pattern inside the code 1 band, the resulting altitude reaching about 280 feet off pattern altitude before the correction took effect. Performance met the desired standard for this stage, and SP is expected to plan the power reduction with the level off so both altitude and speed are captured with a single adjustment.
texts_at.2: SP set and adjusted power through the pattern inside the code 2 band, correcting an excess-energy excursion that had left the aircraft about 220 feet off pattern altitude. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training, and SP is expected to recognize the excess energy a little earlier so the correction is smaller.
texts_at.3: SP set MAX power at the initiation and adjusted it as required at the level off, holding the resulting altitude within about 130 feet of pattern altitude. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus, and SP is expected to anticipate the reduction a little more precisely so both parameters settle together.

texts_above.1: SP set and adjusted power through the pattern, the resulting altitude reaching about 280 feet off pattern altitude. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP recognized the excess energy accelerating the aircraft through the briefed downwind speed and set the correct power without prompting, keeping the resulting altitude within about 220 feet of pattern altitude and without IP input. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady power management through the pattern.
texts_above.3: SP set MAX power at the initiation, confirmed the indication and adjusted power as required at the level off so the downwind was flown at the briefed setting, holding the resulting altitude within about 130 feet of pattern altitude with anticipation rather than reactive correction. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to disciplined power management through the pattern.
texts_above.4: SP applied MAX power smoothly at the initiation and reduced it exactly at the point required for the level off, capturing pattern altitude and downwind airspeed together within about 60 feet with no further adjustment needed. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to first-rate power management through the pattern.

error_modes.label: STALL MARGIN AND AVOIDANCE OF STALL CHARACTERISTICS

texts.0: SP, due to task sequencing that concentrated all cockpit workload inside the turn, increased back pressure to hold the flight path and allowed the onset of stall characteristics. Airframe buffet developed with the stall warning active while the aircraft was banked and climbing, and the margin above the stall was lost rather than protected. The IP took control, unloaded the aircraft and recovered the energy state.
texts.1: SP, due to workload management that left the radio call and the power setting to be completed inside the turn, allowed airspeed to decay to the point where the initial stall warning was heard. SP did not unload the aircraft until the IP called for it, so the margin was restored by direction and not by SP recognition. The pattern was continued only after the energy state had been re-established.
texts.2: SP, due to attention held on the traffic during the turn, allowed airspeed to fall toward the low end of the range for the bank being flown. The margin above the stall was reduced although no stall warning or buffet occurred. SP recognized the decay early, reduced bank and added power without prompting, and the aircraft was returned to the briefed airspeed with no IP input.
texts.3: SP protected the stall margin throughout the closed pattern by matching bank and back pressure to the available power, and no stall characteristics of any kind appeared. Airspeed stayed inside the prescribed range for the bank being flown at every stage of the turn. Secondary tasks were kept out of the highest workload part of the maneuver.
texts.4: SP flew the closed pattern with an ample and constant margin above the stall, with airspeed stable in the upper part of the prescribed range and no buffet or warning indication at any point. Workload was sequenced so that the turn required only flying, with radio and cockpit tasks completed before and after it. The energy state was managed with clear anticipation throughout.
texts.marginal: SP kept the aircraft clear of stall characteristics, but the airspeed reached the lower end of the acceptable range in the second half of each turn before power was added. The margin remained legal while depending on a late correction rather than on planning. SP is expected to sequence the cockpit tasks outside the turn and to protect the airspeed with power from the initiation.

texts_at.0: SP worked the stall margin in the closed pattern, with the IP prompting each action verbally as the item developed, this being SP's first presentation of the item. The Training Section still expects IP assistance for this maneuver at this point, and SP is expected to take over more of the sequence without prompting next time.
texts_at.1: SP protected the stall margin through the closed pattern inside the code 1 band, the resulting level-off deviation reaching about 280 feet before airspeed and bank were corrected. Performance met the desired standard for this stage, and SP is expected to sequence the cockpit tasks outside the turn and protect airspeed with power from the initiation.
texts_at.2: SP protected the stall margin through the closed pattern inside the code 2 band, correcting a margin reduction that had left the resulting level-off deviation at about 220 feet. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training, and SP is expected to recognize the airspeed decay a little earlier in the turn so the margin is restored sooner.
texts_at.3: SP protected the stall margin by matching bank and back pressure to the available power, holding the resulting level-off deviation to about 130 feet with no stall characteristics of any kind appearing. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus, and SP is expected to keep the margin a little wider through the second half of the turn.

texts_above.1: SP protected the stall margin through the closed pattern, the resulting level-off deviation reaching about 280 feet. SP corrected the trend after a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP recognized the airspeed decaying toward the low end of the range and reduced bank while adding power without prompting, holding the resulting level-off deviation to about 220 feet with no IP input. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good stall margin management in the closed pattern.
texts_above.3: SP protected the stall margin throughout the closed pattern by matching bank and back pressure to the available power, holding the resulting level-off deviation to about 130 feet with airspeed inside the prescribed range at every stage of the turn. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good stall margin management in the closed pattern.
texts_above.4: SP flew the closed pattern with an ample and constant margin above the stall, holding the resulting level-off deviation to about 60 feet with airspeed stable in the upper part of the prescribed range throughout. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to excellent stall margin management in the closed pattern.

texts.0: SP, due to reliance on how the maneuver is habitually flown rather than on the published criteria, did not follow the standard procedure of the Techniques and Procedures Manual and the LAP. The closed pattern was initiated without the required clearance and the ground track was flown outside the published pattern limits, with the checks and calls of the procedure omitted. The IP intervened, took control and returned the aircraft to the published pattern.
texts.1: SP, due to an unwritten local practice followed in place of the published procedure, did not execute the closed pattern in the sequence prescribed by the Techniques and Procedures Manual and the LAP. Two required actions were taken out of order and the associated call was made late, which left the pattern at the limit of the published profile until the IP directed the correct sequence. SP complied only after that verbal direction.
texts.2: SP, due to reverting to the habitual sequence rather than the one published for the pattern in use, did not perform the required actions in the correct order at the initiation of the closed pattern. One item of the sequence was completed late in relation to the published procedure, with the resulting altitude deviation inside the 150 to 300 feet band. SP identified the omission on its own and completed the sequence correctly with no IP intervention.
texts.3: SP executed the closed pattern in accordance with the Techniques and Procedures Manual and the applicable LAP, initiating only under the specified conditions and with the required clearance. The sequence of checks, configuration and calls was completed in the correct order and at the correct points. The published ground track was respected throughout.
texts.4: SP executed the closed pattern exactly to the published procedure, with every check, configuration change and call made at the correct point without hesitation and without any reminder. The pattern was flown precisely on the LAP ground track under the specified conditions. SP also stated the applicable procedure correctly when questioned in the debrief.
texts.marginal: SP followed the published procedure and the LAP, but the calls and the required actions were made at the very end of their correct window on each pattern. The sequence was correct in content and consistently late in timing, which compressed the remaining part of the maneuver. SP is expected to complete each item at its published point so that the pattern is not flown under self-imposed time pressure.

texts_at.3: SP executed the closed pattern in accordance with the Techniques and Procedures Manual and the applicable LAP, holding the resulting altitude within about 130 feet of pattern altitude with the sequence of checks and calls completed in the correct order. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus, and SP is expected to complete each item a little earlier in its published window.

The adjustment followed a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP identified an item completed late against the published sequence and corrected it on its own, holding the resulting altitude within about 220 feet of pattern altitude with no IP intervention. error_modes.label: DOWNWIND DISPLACEMENT COMPARED WITH THE OVERHEAD BREAK PATTERN

texts.0: SP, due to a climbing turn flown without reference to the downwind displacement established with an overhead break, did not roll out on the standard downwind track. The aircraft ended up well outside the published downwind line and more than 300 feet off pattern altitude while the runway sight picture was still being searched for. The IP took the controls and repositioned the aircraft on the standard downwind before the pattern could continue.
texts.1: SP, due to holding the initial 60 degrees of bank without checking the runway sight picture, did not match the downwind displacement of the overhead break pattern. Roll out occurred wide of the standard downwind track and altitude reached the 300 feet limit above pattern altitude while the leg was being re-intercepted. The correction was started only after the IP called the displacement.
texts.2: SP, due to a late comparison between the runway sight picture and the displacement used in the overhead break, rolled out slightly outside the standard downwind track. The correction back to the published line left altitude about 200 feet off pattern altitude, between the 150 and 300 feet band. SP recognized the wide roll out early and re-established the correct displacement without prompting and without IP action.
texts.3: SP flew the climbing turn to arrive on the same downwind displacement as the overhead break pattern, using the runway sight picture to judge the roll out point. Track and spacing matched the standard downwind and altitude stayed within 150 feet of pattern altitude throughout. Only small heading adjustments were needed after the roll out.
texts.4: SP rolled out on the standard downwind line, with the displacement indistinguishable from a pattern entered by the overhead break. Altitude at roll out was within about 50 feet of pattern altitude and no lateral correction was required. Spacing for the following approach was set at the roll out and needed no adjustment.
texts.marginal: SP rolled out inside the pattern limits, but the downwind was consistently a little wider than the displacement established with the overhead break and each pattern needed a shallow correction back to the line. Altitude remained inside tolerance only because that correction was flown level. SP is expected to use the runway sight picture during the climbing turn so that the roll out falls on the standard downwind displacement at the first attempt.

texts_at.0: SP practiced the downwind displacement technique, with the IP talking through each step as it was flown, the supporting technique still being built at this point. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage, and SP is expected to rely less on the IP's assistance as the item is repeated.
texts_at.1: SP matched the downwind displacement of the overhead break pattern inside the code 1 band, rolling out with the altitude reaching about 280 feet off pattern altitude while the leg was being re-intercepted. Performance met the desired standard for this stage, and SP is expected to use the runway sight picture during the climbing turn so the roll out falls on the standard downwind at the first attempt.
texts_at.2: SP matched the downwind displacement of the overhead break pattern inside the code 2 band, correcting a wide roll out that had left the altitude about 220 feet off pattern altitude. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training, and SP is expected to compare the sight picture with the displacement earlier in the turn rather than after roll out.
texts_at.3: SP flew the climbing turn to arrive on the same downwind displacement as the overhead break pattern, holding the resulting altitude within about 130 feet of pattern altitude. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus, and SP is expected to judge the roll out point a little more precisely so only a very small heading adjustment is needed.

The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP recognized a wide roll out against the standard downwind track and corrected it without prompting, holding the resulting altitude within about 220 feet of pattern altitude with no IP action. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to superior downwind displacement technique.

error_modes.label: VERTICAL SPEED AT LEVEL OFF AND USE OF BANK UP TO 90 DEGREES

texts.0: SP, due to MAX power carried into a climb rate far higher than the level off could absorb, did not use the available bank to arrest the vertical speed as the manual provides. The climb was still established at pattern altitude and the aircraft passed more than 300 feet above it before any pitch or power change was made. The IP took the controls, reduced power and rolled into bank to stop the climb.
texts.1: SP, due to attempting to stop an excessive vertical speed with pitch alone, did not increase bank toward 90 degrees to affect the level off. The climb was arrested only at the 300 feet limit above pattern altitude and after the IP called for more bank. The aircraft was then held level, but the level off was completed late and high.
texts.2: SP, due to a late power reduction that left the vertical speed high approaching pattern altitude, did not initially use bank to help arrest the climb. Altitude overshot about 200 feet, between the 150 and 300 feet band, before the climb was stopped. SP increased bank without prompting, re-established pattern altitude promptly and no IP input was required.

The only refinement available was to reduce the bank as the airspeed trend showed rather than a fraction after. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to notably good airspeed awareness in the pull-up.
texts_above.4: SP flew every closed pull-up with the airspeed read continuously against the bank, the pull sized so the airspeed never approached the minimum and the level off within a few feet of pattern altitude. The technique is already sound; nothing in the airspeed control needs to change. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to exceptional airspeed awareness in the pull-up.

error_modes.label: Closed pull-up point: clearing the pattern and the runway before the pull, with traffic on downwind and on initial

texts.0: SP, due to a picture of the pattern that did not include the aircraft on inside downwind, requested and started the closed pull-up without clearing the downwind. The pull-up was made into the traffic with the level off more than 300 ft above pattern altitude, with the result that the separation from the downwind traffic was lost. The IP took the controls and rolled the aircraft out of the pull-up.
texts.1: SP, due to the traffic on initial being picked up late, started the closed pull-up as the initial traffic approached the break and leveled off 300 ft above pattern altitude, at the limit of the tolerance, with the result that the sequencing on downwind was resolved by the tower rather than by SP. SP cleared the initial only after the IP called the traffic. The downwind was flown with the spacing regained.
texts.2: SP, due to the clearing of the downwind being completed a beat after the pull-up request, started the pull-up a little before the traffic picture was complete and leveled off about 200 ft above pattern altitude, between the desired and the maximum tolerance, with the result that the spacing on downwind was tighter than planned. SP recognized the traffic during the pull-up, adjusted the level off point and regained the spacing without prompting. The sequencing was maintained.
texts.3: SP cleared the downwind and the initial before requesting the closed pull-up, started the pull at the correct point with the traffic in sight and leveled off within 150 ft of pattern altitude with the spacing as planned. No prompting was required.
texts.4: SP flew the closed pull-up with the traffic picture built before the request, the downwind and the initial cleared and the level off within a few feet of pattern altitude in the planned spacing. Nothing in the clearing needed a correction.
texts.marginal: SP kept the closed pull-up inside the required standard, but the level off sat near the 150 ft high edge of the band on most patterns and the downwind was cleared a beat after the request each time. The tendency is to request the pull-up before the traffic picture is complete. SP is expected to clear the downwind and the initial before the request.

texts_at.0: SP flew the closed pull-up with the IP calling the traffic on downwind and on initial and the pull-up point, since building the traffic picture before the pull-up has not yet been practiced. The pull-up was made without the downwind cleared because the traffic was not yet part of the picture. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance. SP is expected to clear the downwind before the request on the next closed pattern.
texts_at.1: SP started the closed pull-up as the initial traffic approached the break and leveled off about 300 ft above pattern altitude, at the outer edge of the standard, due to the traffic on initial being picked up late. The initial was cleared after the IP called the traffic. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to clear the initial before the pull-up request.
texts_at.2: SP started the pull-up a little before the traffic picture was complete and leveled off about 200 ft above pattern altitude, due to the clearing of the downwind being completed a beat after the request. SP recognized the traffic during the pull-up and regained the spacing without prompting. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to complete the clearing before the request.
texts_at.3: SP cleared the downwind and the initial before the closed pull-up and leveled off within about 120 ft of pattern altitude, due to the pull being started a fraction before the planned point once the clearance was received. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to start the pull at the planned point.

texts_above.1: SP regained the downwind spacing after leveling off about 300 ft above pattern altitude, at the tolerance limit, with the initial traffic in sight through the pull-up. The clearing of the initial followed a verbal call from the IP on the traffic. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP recognized the downwind traffic during the pull-up, adjusted the level off point to about 200 ft above pattern altitude and regained the planned spacing without prompting. Completing the clearing before the request would put the pull-up into a complete traffic picture. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to dependable traffic awareness in the closed pattern.
texts_above.3: SP cleared the downwind and the initial before every closed pull-up request, started the pull with the traffic in sight and leveled off within 120 ft of pattern altitude in the planned spacing. The only refinement available was to start the pull at the planned point rather than a fraction before it. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to precise traffic awareness in the closed pattern.
texts_above.4: SP flew every closed pull-up with the traffic picture built before the request, the downwind and the initial cleared and the level off within a few feet of pattern altitude in the planned spacing. The technique is already sound; nothing in the clearing needs to change. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to exemplary traffic awareness in the closed pattern.

error_modes.label: Crosswind in the closed pull-up: ground track displaced and the closed downwind spacing wide or tight

texts.0: SP, due to the closed pull-up being flown as a fixed heading change with no allowance for the reported crosswind, let the ground track drift with the wind through the climbing turn. The aircraft rolled out on downwind well inside the normal spacing and more than 300 ft above pattern altitude, with the result that the final turn could not be flown from that position. The IP called the go-around.
texts.1: SP, due to the crosswind being allowed for only after the roll-out on downwind, let the ground track drift through the pull-up and rolled out tight to the runway 300 ft above pattern altitude, at the limit of the tolerance, with the result that the downwind had to be displaced outward before the perch. SP corrected the spacing only after the IP called it. The perch was reached with the spacing regained.
texts.2: SP, due to a wind correction in the pull-up a little smaller than the crosswind required, let the ground track drift slightly and rolled out a little tight to the runway about 200 ft above pattern altitude, between the desired and the maximum tolerance, with the result that a small outward displacement was needed on downwind. SP recognized the spacing against the runway, corrected it and regained pattern altitude without prompting. The perch was reached as planned.
texts.3: SP allowed for the crosswind in the closed pull-up, adjusting the bank and the roll-out point so the ground track put the aircraft on the normal downwind spacing within 150 ft of pattern altitude. No prompting was required.
texts.4: SP flew the closed pull-up with the crosswind built into the bank and the roll-out point, arriving on downwind at the planned spacing within a few feet of pattern altitude with no correction needed. Nothing in the wind allowance needed a correction.
texts.marginal: SP kept the closed pull-up inside the required standard with the crosswind, but the downwind spacing ran a little tight and the level off sat near the 150 ft high edge of the band on most patterns. The tendency is to allow for the wind after the roll-out rather than in the pull-up. SP is expected to build the crosswind into the pull-up.

texts_at.0: SP flew the closed pull-up in a crosswind with the IP calling the wind, the bank and the roll-out point, since allowing for the wind in a climbing turn to downwind has not yet been practiced. The aircraft rolled out well inside the normal spacing because the pull-up was flown as a fixed heading change. The maneuver is being introduced at this point of the syllabus, so no independent standard is required yet. SP is expected to adjust the bank for the crosswind on the next closed pattern.
texts_at.1: SP rolled out on downwind tight to the runway and about 300 ft above pattern altitude, at the outer edge of the standard, due to the crosswind being allowed for only after the roll-out. The spacing was corrected after the IP called it. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to allow for the crosswind in the pull-up itself.
texts_at.2: SP rolled out a little tight to the runway about 200 ft above pattern altitude, due to a wind correction in the pull-up a little smaller than the crosswind required. SP recognized the spacing against the runway and corrected without prompting. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to size the wind correction to the reported crosswind.
texts_at.3: SP arrived on downwind at the normal spacing within about 120 ft of pattern altitude with the crosswind, due to the roll-out point being adjusted a fraction less than the drift in the pull-up required. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to adjust the roll-out point for the full drift.

texts_above.1: SP regained the normal downwind spacing before the perch after rolling out tight to the runway about 300 ft above pattern altitude, at the tolerance limit, in the crosswind. The spacing correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP recognized the downwind spacing a little tight against the runway after the closed pull-up about 200 ft above pattern altitude in the crosswind, corrected it and regained pattern altitude without prompting. Sizing the wind correction to the reported crosswind would put the roll-out on the spacing. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to competent wind allowance in the closed pattern.
texts_above.3: SP allowed for the crosswind in every closed pull-up, adjusting the bank and the roll-out point so the ground track put the aircraft on the normal downwind spacing within 120 ft of pattern altitude. The only refinement available was to adjust the roll-out point for the full drift. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate wind allowance in the closed pattern.
texts_above.4: SP flew every closed pull-up with the crosswind built into the bank and the roll-out point, arriving on downwind at the planned spacing within a few feet of pattern altitude with no correction needed. The technique is already sound; nothing in the wind allowance needs to change. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to outstanding wind allowance in the closed pattern.
